arXiv:2604.15497v3 [math.GR] 04 Aug 2026

Homomorphisms of Hecke–Kiselman Monoids Associated to Simple Oriented Graphs

Luka Andrenšek Email: andrensek.luka@gmail.com Affiliation: Department of Mathematics, Faculty of Mathematics and Physics, University of Ljubljana, Jadranska ulica 19, Ljubljana, SI-1000, Slovenia
Abstract

Let Γ\Gamma and Θ\Theta be finite simple oriented graphs, and let 𝐇𝐊Γ\mathbf{HK}_{\Gamma} and 𝐇𝐊Θ\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta} denote the corresponding Hecke–Kiselman monoids. We present a set of Boolean matrices that is in bijection with the set of monoid homomorphisms from 𝐇𝐊Γ\mathbf{HK}_{\Gamma} to 𝐇𝐊Θ\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta}. In particular, we obtain a Boolean matrix monoid isomorphic to the endomorphism monoid of 𝐇𝐊Θ\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta}.

keywords
Hecke–Kiselman monoid, homomorphism, endomorphism monoid, idempotent, Boolean matrix monoid

1 Introduction

Let Θ\Theta be a finite simple oriented graph, that is, a finite oriented graph with no multiple arrows, no loops, and no oriented cycles of length 22. Let VΘ={x1,x2,…,xn}V_{\Theta}=\{x_{1},x_{2},\dots,x_{n}\} be the vertex set of Θ\Theta for some positive integer nn. If there is an arrow from xix_{i} to xjx_{j} in Θ\Theta, we write xi​→Θ​xjx_{i}\overset{\Theta}{\to}x_{j}. For distinct vertices xix_{i} and xjx_{j}, we say that xix_{i} and xjx_{j} are not connected in Θ\Theta if there is no arrow from xix_{i} to xjx_{j} and there is no arrow from xjx_{j} to xix_{i} in Θ\Theta.

In Ganyushkin and Mazorchuk (2011), Ganyushkin and Mazorchuk define the Hecke–Kiselman monoid 𝐇𝐊Θ\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta} associated to Θ\Theta as the monoid generated by

x1,x2,…,xnx_{1},x_{2},\dots,x_{n}

subject to the following defining relations for all xi,xj∈VΘx_{i},x_{j}\in V_{\Theta}:

  • •

    xi2=xix_{i}^{2}=x_{i};

  • •

    xi​xj=xj​xix_{i}x_{j}=x_{j}x_{i} if xix_{i} and xjx_{j} are not connected in Θ\Theta;

  • •

    xi​xj​xi=xj​xi​xj=xi​xjx_{i}x_{j}x_{i}=x_{j}x_{i}x_{j}=x_{i}x_{j} if xi​→Θ​xjx_{i}\overset{\Theta}{\to}x_{j}.

We denote by ee the unit element of 𝐇𝐊Θ\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta}. Let Γ\Gamma be another finite simple oriented graph with vertex set VΓ={y1,y2,…,ym}V_{\Gamma}=\{y_{1},y_{2},\dots,y_{m}\} for some positive integer mm, and let 𝐇𝐊Γ\mathbf{HK}_{\Gamma} denote the corresponding Hecke–Kiselman monoid.

This paper studies the set of all monoid homomorphisms from 𝐇𝐊Γ\mathbf{HK}_{\Gamma} to 𝐇𝐊Θ\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta}, which we denote by Hom⁡(𝐇𝐊Γ,𝐇𝐊Θ)\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbf{HK}_{\Gamma},\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta}), and the endomorphism monoid End⁡(𝐇𝐊Θ)\mathrm{End}(\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta}) whose operation is the usual composition of maps. Throughout, monoid homomorphisms are assumed to preserve the identity element.

Hecke–Kiselman monoids were originally introduced in the setting of finite simple digraphs Ganyushkin and Mazorchuk (2011). They are a natural mixture of two families of monoids, namely, 0-Hecke monoids, which are closely connected to Coxeter groups, and Kiselman monoids Kiselman (2002); Kudryavtseva and Mazorchuk (2009). They have been studied by various authors Aragona and D’Andrea (2013); Aragona and D’Andrea (2020); Ashikhmin et al. (2015); Collina and D’Andrea (2015); Forsberg (2017); Ganyushkin and Mazorchuk (2011); Lebed (2025); Wiertel (2024). Particular interest has been devoted to the corresponding Hecke–Kiselman algebras Okniński and Wiertel (2020); Okniński and Wiertel (2021); Wiertel (2022); Wiertel (2023). In this paper, we only consider Hecke–Kiselman monoids associated to simple oriented graphs.

From the proof of (Ganyushkin and Mazorchuk, 2011, Theorem 16), it follows that monoid isomorphisms from 𝐇𝐊Γ\mathbf{HK}_{\Gamma} to 𝐇𝐊Θ\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta} are in bijection with graph isomorphisms from Γ\Gamma to Θ\Theta. Setting Γ=Θ\Gamma=\Theta, it can be verified that the automorphism group of 𝐇𝐊Θ\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta} is isomorphic to the automorphism group of the graph Θ\Theta. To the best of our knowledge, general monoid homomorphisms from 𝐇𝐊Γ\mathbf{HK}_{\Gamma} to 𝐇𝐊Θ\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta} and the structure of the endomorphism monoid of 𝐇𝐊Θ\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta} have not been systematically studied in the literature. However, a description of endomorphisms of the Kiselman monoid, which is the Hecke–Kiselman monoid corresponding to the complete acyclic oriented graph, is known in the literature Andrenšek (2026).

The main result of this paper is Theorem 4.5. We show that Hom⁡(𝐇𝐊Γ,𝐇𝐊Θ)\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbf{HK}_{\Gamma},\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta}) is in bijection with the set of Boolean matrices corresponding to (Γ,Θ)(\Gamma,\Theta)-admissible sequences of sets, which are defined in Definition 4.2. These are finite sequences of length mm of subsets of VΘV_{\Theta} for which the induced full subgraphs of Θ\Theta do not contain any oriented cycles, and which satisfy a simple graph-theoretic condition, later denoted by pΘp_{\Theta} and defined in Definition 3.1, according to arrows in Γ\Gamma. Furthermore, in Theorem 5.4, we show that in the case Γ=Θ\Gamma=\Theta, the constructed bijection between End⁡(𝐇𝐊Θ)\mathrm{End}(\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta}) and the corresponding Boolean matrices is a monoid isomorphism.

The paper is organised as follows. In Section 2, we establish basic notation and recall results from the relevant literature. In Section 3, we prove new results on idempotents in 𝐇𝐊Θ\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta}. These results are used to prove the main result in Section 4, and we consider the endomorphism monoid of 𝐇𝐊Θ\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta} in Section 5.

2 Preliminaries

Denote by F⁡(VΘ)F(V_{\Theta}) the free monoid over the alphabet VΘ={x1,x2,…,xn}V_{\Theta}=\{x_{1},x_{2},\dots,x_{n}\}. Elements of F⁡(VΘ)F(V_{\Theta}) are called words, and each xi∈VΘx_{i}\in V_{\Theta} is called a letter. In what follows, we will use the term letter to refer to the vertices of Θ\Theta, generators of 𝐇𝐊Θ\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta}, and generators of F⁡(VΘ)F(V_{\Theta}). We have the canonical projection

π:F⁡(VΘ)↠𝐇𝐊Θ.\pi:F(V_{\Theta})\twoheadrightarrow\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta}.

For a word w∈F⁡(VΘ)w\in F(V_{\Theta}), denote by ℓ⁡(w)\ell(w) its length. The unique word of length 00 is called the empty word.

2.1 The Content Map

For a word w∈F⁡(VΘ)w\in F(V_{\Theta}), we define its content c⁡(w)c(w) as the set of xi∈VΘx_{i}\in V_{\Theta} for which xix_{i} appears in ww. Since the defining relations of 𝐇𝐊Θ\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta} preserve content, we can define the content and denote it again by c⁡(x)c(x) for x∈𝐇𝐊Θx\in\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta} as the content of any word w∈F⁡(VΘ)w\in F(V_{\Theta}) with x=π⁡(w)x=\pi(w). Moreover, we have

c⁡(x​y)=c⁡(x)∪c⁡(y)andc⁡(e)=∅,c(xy)=c(x)\cup c(y)\quad\text{and}\quad c(e)=\emptyset,

which shows that c:𝐇𝐊Θ↠𝟚VΘc:\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta}\twoheadrightarrow\mathbbm{2}^{V_{\Theta}} is a monoid epimorphism, where 𝟚VΘ\mathbbm{2}^{V_{\Theta}} is equipped with the operation ∪\cup.

We use the following lemma in the proof of Proposition 5.1.

Lemma 2.1.

Let ψ,φ∈End⁡(𝐇𝐊Θ)\psi,\varphi\in\mathrm{End}(\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta}) and xi∈𝐇𝐊Θx_{i}\in\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta}. Then

c⁡((ψ∘φ)​(xi))=⋃xj∈c⁡(φ⁡(xi))c⁡(ψ⁡(xj)).c((\psi\circ\varphi)(x_{i}))=\bigcup_{x_{j}\in c(\varphi(x_{i}))}c(\psi(x_{j})).
Proof.

If φ⁡(xi)=e\varphi(x_{i})=e, then we have c⁡(φ⁡(xi))=∅c(\varphi(x_{i}))=\emptyset and (ψ∘φ)​(xi)=e(\psi\circ\varphi)(x_{i})=e. Hence c⁡((ψ∘φ)​(xi))=∅c((\psi\circ\varphi)(x_{i}))=\emptyset, and thus the conclusion holds in this case.

Now suppose φ⁡(xi)≠e\varphi(x_{i})\neq e and write φ⁡(xi)=xi1​…​xik\varphi(x_{i})=x_{i_{1}}\dots x_{i_{k}} for some letters xi1,…,xik∈𝐇𝐊Θx_{i_{1}},\dots,x_{i_{k}}\in\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta} and k≥1k\geq 1. Then c⁡(φ⁡(xi))={xi1,…,xik}c(\varphi(x_{i}))=\{x_{i_{1}},\dots,x_{i_{k}}\} and we further have

(ψ∘φ)​(xi)=ψ⁡(φ⁡(xi))=ψ⁡(xi1​…​xik)=ψ⁡(xi1)​…​ψ​(xik).(\psi\circ\varphi)(x_{i})=\psi(\varphi(x_{i}))=\psi(x_{i_{1}}\dots x_{i_{k}})=\psi(x_{i_{1}})\dots\psi(x_{i_{k}}).

Hence we have

c⁡((ψ∘φ)​(xi))=c⁡(ψ⁡(xi1))∪⋯∪c⁡(ψ⁡(xik)),c((\psi\circ\varphi)(x_{i}))=c(\psi(x_{i_{1}}))\cup\dots\cup c(\psi(x_{i_{k}})),

and therefore,

c⁡((ψ∘φ)​(xi))=⋃xj∈{xi1,…,xik}c⁡(ψ⁡(xj))=⋃xj∈c⁡(φ⁡(xi))c⁡(ψ⁡(xj)).c((\psi\circ\varphi)(x_{i}))=\bigcup_{x_{j}\in\{x_{i_{1}},\dots,x_{i_{k}}\}}c(\psi(x_{j}))=\bigcup_{x_{j}\in c(\varphi(x_{i}))}c(\psi(x_{j})).

∎

2.2 Normal Forms in 𝐇𝐊Θ\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta}

Here we recall the main results from Aragona and D’Andrea (2020). The following lemma is proved in (Aragona and D’Andrea, 2020, Lemma 1).

Lemma 2.2.

If xi∈𝐇𝐊Θx_{i}\in\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta} is a letter and w∈𝐇𝐊Θw\in\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta} is obtained by multiplying letters that do not admit arrows to (respectively from) xix_{i}, then xi​w​xi=xi​wx_{i}wx_{i}=x_{i}w (respectively xi​w​xi=w​xix_{i}wx_{i}=wx_{i}).

The right cancellation →𝑟\overset{r}{\to} and left cancellation →𝑙\overset{l}{\to} are binary relations on F⁡(VΘ)F(V_{\Theta}) defined as follows. For w,w′∈F⁡(VΘ)w,w^{\prime}\in F(V_{\Theta}), we have

  • •

    w​→𝑟​w′w\overset{r}{\to}w^{\prime} if there exist words w1,w2,u∈F⁡(VΘ)w_{1},w_{2},u\in F(V_{\Theta}), and a letter xi∈F⁡(VΘ)x_{i}\in F(V_{\Theta}) such that w=w1​xi​u​xi​w2w=w_{1}x_{i}ux_{i}w_{2}, w′=w1​xi​u​w2w^{\prime}=w_{1}x_{i}uw_{2}, and no letter in uu has an arrow to xix_{i}.

  • •

    w​→𝑙​w′w\overset{l}{\to}w^{\prime} if there exist words w1,w2,u∈F⁡(VΘ)w_{1},w_{2},u\in F(V_{\Theta}), and a letter xi∈F⁡(VΘ)x_{i}\in F(V_{\Theta}) such that w=w1​xi​u​xi​w2w=w_{1}x_{i}ux_{i}w_{2}, w′=w1​u​xi​w2w^{\prime}=w_{1}ux_{i}w_{2}, and no letter in uu has an arrow from xix_{i}.

Right and left cancellations are also called elementary cancellations. Denote by →=→𝑟∪→𝑙\to=\overset{r}{\to}\cup\overset{l}{\to} and let →∗\overset{*}{\to} be the reflexive-transitive closure of →\to on F⁡(VΘ)F(V_{\Theta}). Then Lemma 2.2 implies that for u,v∈F⁡(VΘ)u,v\in F(V_{\Theta}), if u→vu\to v, then π⁡(u)=π⁡(v)\pi(u)=\pi(v). Therefore, if w​→∗​w′w\overset{*}{\to}w^{\prime} for w,w′∈F⁡(VΘ)w,w^{\prime}\in F(V_{\Theta}), then π⁡(w)=π⁡(w′)\pi(w)=\pi(w^{\prime}).

Definition 2.3.

A word w∈F⁡(VΘ)w\in F(V_{\Theta}) is a normal form of x∈𝐇𝐊Θx\in\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta} if x=π⁡(w)x=\pi(w) and no elementary cancellations may be performed on ww.

Every x∈𝐇𝐊Θx\in\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta} has at least one normal form, as any word of minimal length in π−1​({x})\pi^{-1}(\{x\}) must be a normal form of xx. Denote by 𝒩\mathcal{N} the set of all normal forms of all elements of 𝐇𝐊Θ\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta}.

Define the equivalence relation ∼\sim on F⁡(VΘ)F(V_{\Theta}), which is generated by elementary commutations:

w1​xi​xj​w2∼w1​xj​xi​w2,w_{1}x_{i}x_{j}w_{2}\sim w_{1}x_{j}x_{i}w_{2},

for all words w1,w2∈F⁡(VΘ)w_{1},w_{2}\in F(V_{\Theta}), and letters xi,xj∈F⁡(VΘ)x_{i},x_{j}\in F(V_{\Theta}) such that xix_{i} and xjx_{j} are not connected in Θ\Theta. The following was proved in (Aragona and D’Andrea, 2020, Theorem 1).

Theorem 2.4.

The following statements hold.

  1. (i)

    Let w,w′∈F⁡(VΘ)w,w^{\prime}\in F(V_{\Theta}). If π⁡(w)=π⁡(w′)\pi(w)=\pi(w^{\prime}) and u,v∈𝒩u,v\in\mathcal{N} satisfy w​→∗​uw\overset{*}{\to}u and w′​→∗​vw^{\prime}\overset{*}{\to}v, then u∼vu\sim v.

  2. (ii)

    Every simplifying sequence

    w→w1→w2→…→wkw\to w_{1}\to w_{2}\to\dots\to w_{k}

    may be extended to a simplifying sequence ending on a normal form of π⁡(w)\pi(w).

2.3 Idempotents in 𝐇𝐊Θ\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta}

For X⊆VΘX\subseteq V_{\Theta}, denote by Θ⁡[X]\Theta[X] the full subgraph of Θ\Theta with vertex set XX, that is, Θ⁡[X]\Theta[X] is an oriented graph with vertex set XX and for xi,xj∈Xx_{i},x_{j}\in X, there is an arrow from xix_{i} to xjx_{j} in Θ⁡[X]\Theta[X] if and only if there is an arrow from xix_{i} to xjx_{j} in Θ\Theta.

In (Forsberg, 2017, Theorem 3.6), the following theorem is proved for a general finite simple oriented graph Θ\Theta.

Theorem 2.5.

There is a bijection between idempotents in 𝐇𝐊Θ\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta} and full subgraphs of Θ\Theta which do not contain any oriented cycles.

In the proof, an idempotent is mapped to the full subgraph of Θ\Theta whose vertex set is the content of the idempotent. Therefore, for each X⊆VΘX\subseteq V_{\Theta} such that Θ⁡[X]\Theta[X] does not contain any oriented cycles, there exists exactly one idempotent in 𝐇𝐊Θ\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta} with content XX. We denote this idempotent by eXe_{X}.

We denote the following set

𝒜Θ={X⊆VΘ∣Θ⁡[X]​ does not contain any oriented cycles}.\mathcal{A}_{\Theta}=\{X\subseteq V_{\Theta}\mid\Theta[X]\text{ does not contain any oriented cycles}\}.
Remark 2.6.

If Y⊆X∈𝒜ΘY\subseteq X\in\mathcal{A}_{\Theta}, then Θ⁡[Y]\Theta[Y] is a subgraph of Θ⁡[X]\Theta[X], and hence it does not contain any oriented cycles. Therefore, Y∈𝒜ΘY\in\mathcal{A}_{\Theta}.

Theorem 2.5 implies the following proposition.

Proposition 2.7.

The set

{eX∣X∈𝒜Θ}\{e_{X}\mid X\in\mathcal{A}_{\Theta}\}

is the set of all idempotents in 𝐇𝐊Θ\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta}.

Proposition 2.8.

Let X,Y∈𝒜ΘX,Y\in\mathcal{A}_{\Theta}. Then eX​eYe_{X}e_{Y} is an idempotent in 𝐇𝐊Θ\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta} if and only if X∪Y∈𝒜ΘX\cup Y\in\mathcal{A}_{\Theta} and eX​eY=eX∪Ye_{X}e_{Y}=e_{X\cup Y}.

Proof.

If X∪Y∈𝒜ΘX\cup Y\in\mathcal{A}_{\Theta} and eX​eY=eX∪Ye_{X}e_{Y}=e_{X\cup Y}, then eX​eYe_{X}e_{Y} is an idempotent by Proposition 2.7. Conversely, if eX​eYe_{X}e_{Y} is an idempotent, then by Proposition 2.7, there exists Z∈𝒜ΘZ\in\mathcal{A}_{\Theta} such that

eX​eY=eZ.e_{X}e_{Y}=e_{Z}.

Taking contents, we get

Z=c⁡(eZ)=c⁡(eX​eY)=c⁡(eX)∪c⁡(eY)=X∪Y.Z=c(e_{Z})=c(e_{X}e_{Y})=c(e_{X})\cup c(e_{Y})=X\cup Y.

Hence X∪Y∈𝒜ΘX\cup Y\in\mathcal{A}_{\Theta} and eX​eY=eX∪Ye_{X}e_{Y}=e_{X\cup Y}. ∎

The idempotent eXe_{X} can be written explicitly. Note that if Θ⁡[X]\Theta[X] does not contain any oriented cycles, then we can write XX as X={xi1,xi2,…,xik}X=\{x_{i_{1}},x_{i_{2}},\dots,x_{i_{k}}\} such that xij​→Θ​xij′x_{i_{j}}\overset{\Theta}{\to}x_{i_{j^{\prime}}} implies j<j′j<j^{\prime} for all j,j′∈{1,2,…,k}j,j^{\prime}\in\{1,2,\dots,k\}.

Lemma 2.9.

Let X∈𝒜ΘX\in\mathcal{A}_{\Theta}. Then for any ordering of the set X={xi1,xi2,…,xik}X=\{x_{i_{1}},x_{i_{2}},\dots,x_{i_{k}}\} such that xij​→Θ​xij′x_{i_{j}}\overset{\Theta}{\to}x_{i_{j^{\prime}}} implies j<j′j<j^{\prime} for all j,j′∈{1,2,…,k}j,j^{\prime}\in\{1,2,\dots,k\}, we have

eX=xi1​xi2​…​xik.e_{X}=x_{i_{1}}x_{i_{2}}\dots x_{i_{k}}.

Moreover, we have eX​z=z​eX=eXe_{X}z=ze_{X}=e_{X} for any z∈𝐇𝐊Θz\in\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta} with c⁡(z)⊆Xc(z)\subseteq X.

Proof.

Denote by

y=xi1​xi2​…​xik.y=x_{i_{1}}x_{i_{2}}\dots x_{i_{k}}.

If xij∈Xx_{i_{j}}\in X, then

xij+1​xij+2​…​xikx_{i_{j+1}}x_{i_{j+2}}\dots x_{i_{k}}

is obtained by multiplying letters that do not admit arrows to xijx_{i_{j}}. Lemma 2.2 implies

y​xij=xi1​…​xij−1​(xij​xij+1​…​xik​xij)=xi1​…​xij−1​(xij​xij+1​…​xik)=y.yx_{i_{j}}=x_{i_{1}}\dots x_{i_{j-1}}(x_{i_{j}}x_{i_{j+1}}\dots x_{i_{k}}x_{i_{j}})=x_{i_{1}}\dots x_{i_{j-1}}(x_{i_{j}}x_{i_{j+1}}\dots x_{i_{k}})=y.

By induction, we get

y​xl1​xl2​…​xlm=y,yx_{l_{1}}x_{l_{2}}\dots x_{l_{m}}=y,

for any xl1,xl2,…,xlm∈Xx_{l_{1}},x_{l_{2}},\dots,x_{l_{m}}\in X. This proves y​z=yyz=y for any z∈𝐇𝐊Θz\in\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta} with c⁡(z)⊆Xc(z)\subseteq X.

For any xij∈Xx_{i_{j}}\in X,

xi1​xi2​…​xij−1x_{i_{1}}x_{i_{2}}\dots x_{i_{j-1}}

is obtained by multiplying letters that do not admit arrows from xijx_{i_{j}}. Lemma 2.2 implies

xij​y=(xij​xi1​…​xij−1​xij)​xij+1​…​xik=(xi1​…​xij−1​xij)​xij+1​…​xik=y.x_{i_{j}}y=(x_{i_{j}}x_{i_{1}}\dots x_{i_{j-1}}x_{i_{j}})x_{i_{j+1}}\dots x_{i_{k}}=(x_{i_{1}}\dots x_{i_{j-1}}x_{i_{j}})x_{i_{j+1}}\dots x_{i_{k}}=y.

By induction, we again obtain

xl1​xl2​…​xlm​y=y,x_{l_{1}}x_{l_{2}}\dots x_{l_{m}}y=y,

for any xl1,xl2,…,xlm∈Xx_{l_{1}},x_{l_{2}},\dots,x_{l_{m}}\in X, which proves z​y=yzy=y for any z∈𝐇𝐊Θz\in\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta} with c⁡(z)⊆Xc(z)\subseteq X. Since c⁡(y)=Xc(y)=X, we have

y2=y​y=y.y^{2}=yy=y.

Hence yy is an idempotent in 𝐇𝐊Θ\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta}. Since c⁡(y)=Xc(y)=X, it follows that y=eXy=e_{X}. ∎

Definition 2.10.

A word w∈F⁡(VΘ)w\in F(V_{\Theta}) is said to have no arrows from right to left if

w=xi1​xi2​…​xik,w=x_{i_{1}}x_{i_{2}}\dots x_{i_{k}},

where xi1,xi2,…,xik∈F⁡(VΘ)x_{i_{1}},x_{i_{2}},\dots,x_{i_{k}}\in F(V_{\Theta}) are letters, and if there is an arrow from xijx_{i_{j}} to xij′x_{i_{j^{\prime}}} then j<j′j<j^{\prime} for all j,j′∈{1,2,…,k}j,j^{\prime}\in\{1,2,\dots,k\}.

Moreover, for X∈𝒜ΘX\in\mathcal{A}_{\Theta}, ww is said to be XX-topological if ww has no arrows from right to left, c⁡(w)=Xc(w)=X, and ℓ⁡(w)=|X|\ell(w)=|X|. In other words, ww is XX-topological if there are no arrows from right to left and each letter xix_{i} with xi∈Xx_{i}\in X occurs in ww exactly once.

Remark 2.11.

If X∈𝒜ΘX\in\mathcal{A}_{\Theta}, then Θ⁡[X]\Theta[X] is an acyclic oriented graph and hence there exists an XX-topological word. Also observe that the empty word is ∅\emptyset-topological.

Lemma 2.12.

For X∈𝒜ΘX\in\mathcal{A}_{\Theta}, a word w∈F⁡(VΘ)w\in F(V_{\Theta}) is XX-topological if and only if ww is a normal form of eXe_{X}.

Proof.

If ww is XX-topological, then π⁡(w)=eX\pi(w)=e_{X} by Lemma 2.9. Moreover, since no letter in ww occurs more than once, no further elementary cancellations may be performed on ww, and hence ww is a normal form of eXe_{X}.

Now assume ww is a normal form of eXe_{X}. Since X∈𝒜ΘX\in\mathcal{A}_{\Theta}, there exists an XX-topological word vv by Remark 2.11. Hence, there are no arrows from right to left in vv, c⁡(v)=Xc(v)=X, and ℓ⁡(v)=|X|\ell(v)=|X|. By the previous paragraph, vv is a normal form of eXe_{X}. By Theorem 2.4 (i), we have w∼vw\sim v. Since elementary commutations only interchange letters that are not connected, the relative order of any two letters that are connected by an arrow is preserved under ∼\sim. Hence, since vv has no arrows from right to left, the same is true for ww. Since ∼\sim also preserves content and length, we have c⁡(w)=c⁡(v)=Xc(w)=c(v)=X and ℓ⁡(w)=ℓ⁡(v)=|X|\ell(w)=\ell(v)=|X|. This implies that ww is XX-topological. ∎

Lemma 2.13.

Let X,Y∈𝒜ΘX,Y\in\mathcal{A}_{\Theta}. If there are no arrows starting in YY and ending in XX and X∩Y=∅X\cap Y=\emptyset, then X∪Y∈𝒜ΘX\cup Y\in\mathcal{A}_{\Theta} and

eX​eY=eX∪Y.e_{X}e_{Y}=e_{X\cup Y}.
Proof.

Since X∩Y=∅X\cap Y=\emptyset and there are no arrows starting in YY and ending in XX, any oriented cycle in Θ⁡[X∪Y]\Theta[X\cup Y] must entirely lie in either XX or YY. Since X,Y∈𝒜ΘX,Y\in\mathcal{A}_{\Theta}, it follows that there are no oriented cycles in Θ⁡[X∪Y]\Theta[X\cup Y], and hence X∪Y∈𝒜ΘX\cup Y\in\mathcal{A}_{\Theta}. Let wXw_{X} be a normal form of eXe_{X} and let wYw_{Y} be a normal form of eYe_{Y}. Lemma 2.12 implies that wXw_{X} is XX-topological and wYw_{Y} is YY-topological. Since there are no arrows from right to left in wXw_{X} and wYw_{Y}, respectively, and there are no arrows starting in YY and ending in XX, there are no arrows from right to left in the word wX​wYw_{X}w_{Y}. Moreover, we have

c⁡(wX​wY)=c⁡(wX)∪c⁡(wY)=X∪Y,c(w_{X}w_{Y})=c(w_{X})\cup c(w_{Y})=X\cup Y,

and

ℓ⁡(wX​wY)=ℓ⁡(wX)+ℓ⁡(wY)=|X|+|Y|=|X∪Y|.\ell(w_{X}w_{Y})=\ell(w_{X})+\ell(w_{Y})=|X|+|Y|=|X\cup Y|.

Hence wX​wYw_{X}w_{Y} is X∪YX\cup Y-topological. Therefore, Lemma 2.12 implies that wX​wYw_{X}w_{Y} is a normal form of eX∪Ye_{X\cup Y}, and hence

eX​eY=π⁡(wX)​π​(wY)=π⁡(wX​wY)=eX∪Y.e_{X}e_{Y}=\pi(w_{X})\pi(w_{Y})=\pi(w_{X}w_{Y})=e_{X\cup Y}.

∎

3 Properties of Idempotents in 𝐇𝐊Θ\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta}

In this section, we give some additional properties of idempotents in 𝐇𝐊Θ\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta}, which are used in Section 4.

Definition 3.1.

For X,Y∈𝒜ΘX,Y\in\mathcal{A}_{\Theta}, define the predicate pΘp_{\Theta} as follows. Condition pΘ​(X,Y)p_{\Theta}(X,Y) holds if and only if there do not exist xb∈Y∖Xx_{b}\in Y\setminus X, xa∈X∖Yx_{a}\in X\setminus Y, r∈ℕ0r\in\mathbb{N}_{0}, and xi1,…,xir∈X∩Yx_{i_{1}},\dots,x_{i_{r}}\in X\cap Y such that

xb​→Θ​xi1​→Θ​…​→Θ​xir​→Θ​xa.x_{b}\overset{\Theta}{\to}x_{i_{1}}\overset{\Theta}{\to}\dots\overset{\Theta}{\to}x_{i_{r}}\overset{\Theta}{\to}x_{a}.
Remark 3.2.

If r=0r=0, a chain xb​→Θ​xi1​→Θ​…​→Θ​xir​→Θ​xax_{b}\overset{\Theta}{\to}x_{i_{1}}\overset{\Theta}{\to}\dots\overset{\Theta}{\to}x_{i_{r}}\overset{\Theta}{\to}x_{a} is interpreted as xb​→Θ​xax_{b}\overset{\Theta}{\to}x_{a}.

Lemma 3.3.

Let X,Y∈𝒜ΘX,Y\in\mathcal{A}_{\Theta}. Then pΘ​(X,Y)p_{\Theta}(X,Y) holds if and only if there does not exist a directed path in Θ⁡[X∪Y]\Theta[X\cup Y] whose startpoint lies in Y∖XY\setminus X and whose endpoint lies in X∖YX\setminus Y.

Proof.

If there is no directed path in Θ⁡[X∪Y]\Theta[X\cup Y] which starts in some vertex of Y∖XY\setminus X and ends in some vertex of X∖YX\setminus Y, then pΘ​(X,Y)p_{\Theta}(X,Y) must hold. Assume pΘ​(X,Y)p_{\Theta}(X,Y) holds. Suppose there exists a directed path

xi1​→Θ​xi2​→Θ​…​→Θ​xik,x_{i_{1}}\overset{\Theta}{\to}x_{i_{2}}\overset{\Theta}{\to}\dots\overset{\Theta}{\to}x_{i_{k}},

such that xi1∈Y∖Xx_{i_{1}}\in Y\setminus X, xik∈X∖Yx_{i_{k}}\in X\setminus Y, and xi1,xi2,…,xik∈X∪Yx_{i_{1}},x_{i_{2}},\dots,x_{i_{k}}\in X\cup Y. Let

j1=max⁡{j∈{1,…,k}∣xij∈Y∖X}andj2=min⁡{j∈{j1+1,…,k}∣xij∈X∖Y}.j_{1}=\max\{j\in\{1,\dots,k\}\mid x_{i_{j}}\in Y\setminus X\}\quad\text{and}\quad j_{2}=\min\{j\in\{j_{1}+1,\dots,k\}\mid x_{i_{j}}\in X\setminus Y\}.

Since xik∈X∖Yx_{i_{k}}\in X\setminus Y and j1<kj_{1}<k, the index j2j_{2} is well-defined, and j1<j2j_{1}<j_{2}. Then the directed path

xij1​→Θ​xij1+1​→Θ​…​→Θ​xij2−1​→Θ​xij2x_{i_{j_{1}}}\overset{\Theta}{\to}x_{i_{j_{1}+1}}\overset{\Theta}{\to}\dots\overset{\Theta}{\to}x_{i_{j_{2}-1}}\overset{\Theta}{\to}x_{i_{j_{2}}}

starts in Y∖XY\setminus X and ends in X∖YX\setminus Y. Moreover, the vertices xij1+1,…,xij2−1x_{i_{j_{1}+1}},\dots,x_{i_{j_{2}-1}} lie in X∩YX\cap Y; by the maximality of j1j_{1}, none of them lies in Y∖XY\setminus X, and by the minimality of j2j_{2}, none of them lies in X∖YX\setminus Y. Since all vertices of the directed path lie in X∪YX\cup Y, the vertices xij1+1,…,xij2−1x_{i_{j_{1}+1}},\dots,x_{i_{j_{2}-1}} must lie in X∩YX\cap Y. This contradicts the fact that pΘ​(X,Y)p_{\Theta}(X,Y) holds and concludes the proof. ∎

Let w=xi1​xi2​…​xik∈F⁡(VΘ)w=x_{i_{1}}x_{i_{2}}\dots x_{i_{k}}\in F(V_{\Theta}) be a word, where xi1,xi2,…,xik∈F⁡(VΘ)x_{i_{1}},x_{i_{2}},\dots,x_{i_{k}}\in F(V_{\Theta}) are letters. A word of the form u=xij1​xij2​…​xijlu=x_{i_{j_{1}}}x_{i_{j_{2}}}\dots x_{i_{j_{l}}} with 1≤j1<j2<⋯<jl≤k1\leq j_{1}<j_{2}<\dots<j_{l}\leq k is called a quasi-subword of ww. Moreover, the empty word is a quasi-subword of any word. From the definition of →\to, it follows that if u​→∗​vu\overset{*}{\to}v, then vv is a quasi-subword of uu.

Proposition 3.4.

Let X,Y∈𝒜ΘX,Y\in\mathcal{A}_{\Theta}. If eX​eYe_{X}e_{Y} is an idempotent in 𝐇𝐊Θ\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta}, then pΘ​(X,Y)p_{\Theta}(X,Y) holds.

Proof.

Assume pΘ​(X,Y)p_{\Theta}(X,Y) does not hold. We show that eX​eYe_{X}e_{Y} is not an idempotent. Suppose that, on the contrary, eX​eYe_{X}e_{Y} is an idempotent. We now construct a contradiction. Let wXw_{X} be a normal form of eXe_{X} and let wYw_{Y} be a normal form of eYe_{Y}. Lemma 2.12 implies that wXw_{X} is XX-topological and wYw_{Y} is YY-topological. We also have π⁡(wX​wY)=eX​eY\pi(w_{X}w_{Y})=e_{X}e_{Y}. Since eX​eYe_{X}e_{Y} is an idempotent, by Proposition 2.8, we have

X∪Y∈𝒜ΘandeX​eY=eX∪Y.X\cup Y\in\mathcal{A}_{\Theta}\quad\text{and}\quad e_{X}e_{Y}=e_{X\cup Y}.

Let u∈F⁡(VΘ)u\in F(V_{\Theta}) be a normal form of eX∪Ye_{X\cup Y} with wX​wY​→∗​uw_{X}w_{Y}\overset{*}{\to}u. Such a word uu exists by Theorem 2.4 (ii) and π⁡(wX​wY)=eX​eY=eX∪Y\pi(w_{X}w_{Y})=e_{X}e_{Y}=e_{X\cup Y}. By Lemma 2.12, uu is X∪YX\cup Y-topological.

Since pΘ​(X,Y)p_{\Theta}(X,Y) does not hold, there exist xb∈Y∖Xx_{b}\in Y\setminus X, xa∈X∖Yx_{a}\in X\setminus Y, r∈ℕ0r\in\mathbb{N}_{0}, and xi1,…,xir∈X∩Yx_{i_{1}},\dots,x_{i_{r}}\in X\cap Y such that

xb​→Θ​xi1​→Θ​…​→Θ​xir​→Θ​xa.x_{b}\overset{\Theta}{\to}x_{i_{1}}\overset{\Theta}{\to}\dots\overset{\Theta}{\to}x_{i_{r}}\overset{\Theta}{\to}x_{a}.

Observe that each of the letters xax_{a} and xbx_{b} occurs exactly once in wX​wYw_{X}w_{Y}, and hence they occur exactly once in uu, since an elementary cancellation cannot delete a letter that occurs only once. Moreover, xax_{a} occurs to the left of xbx_{b} in wX​wYw_{X}w_{Y}, since xax_{a} occurs in wXw_{X} and xbx_{b} occurs in wYw_{Y}. Since wX​wY​→∗​uw_{X}w_{Y}\overset{*}{\to}u, uu is a quasi-subword of wX​wYw_{X}w_{Y}, and hence xax_{a} occurs to the left of xbx_{b} in uu as well.

If r=0r=0, then xb​→Θ​xax_{b}\overset{\Theta}{\to}x_{a}. Hence xax_{a} must occur to the right of xbx_{b} in uu, since there are no arrows from right to left in uu, as uu is X∪YX\cup Y-topological. This contradicts the last conclusion of the previous paragraph, which established that xax_{a} occurs to the left of xbx_{b} in uu. Now assume r>0r>0. Since uu is X∪YX\cup Y-topological and xi1,…,xir∈X∩Y⊆X∪Yx_{i_{1}},\dots,x_{i_{r}}\in X\cap Y\subseteq X\cup Y, each of the letters xi1,…,xirx_{i_{1}},\dots,x_{i_{r}} occurs exactly once in uu. Since xb​→Θ​xi1x_{b}\overset{\Theta}{\to}x_{i_{1}} and uu has no arrows from right to left, xi1x_{i_{1}} occurs to the right of xbx_{b} in uu. It follows that for 1<t≤r1<t\leq r, xitx_{i_{t}} occurs to the right of xit−1x_{i_{t-1}} in uu, since xit−1​→Θ​xitx_{i_{t-1}}\overset{\Theta}{\to}x_{i_{t}} and uu has no arrows from right to left. Inductively, we conclude that each xitx_{i_{t}} for 1≤t≤r1\leq t\leq r occurs to the right of xbx_{b} in uu. Finally, it follows from xir​→Θ​xax_{i_{r}}\overset{\Theta}{\to}x_{a} and the fact that uu has no arrows from right to left that xax_{a} occurs to the right of xirx_{i_{r}} in uu, and hence xax_{a} occurs to the right of xbx_{b} in uu. In the previous paragraph, however, it is established that xax_{a} occurs to the left of xbx_{b} in uu. Hence we have reached a contradiction, and the proof is complete. ∎

Proposition 3.5.

Let X,Y∈𝒜ΘX,Y\in\mathcal{A}_{\Theta}. If pΘ​(X,Y)p_{\Theta}(X,Y) holds, then eX​eYe_{X}e_{Y} is an idempotent in 𝐇𝐊Θ\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta}.

Proof.

Assume pΘ​(X,Y)p_{\Theta}(X,Y) holds. To prove that eX​eYe_{X}e_{Y} is an idempotent, by Proposition 2.8, we need to show X∪Y∈𝒜ΘX\cup Y\in\mathcal{A}_{\Theta} and eX​eY=eX∪Ye_{X}e_{Y}=e_{X\cup Y}.

Denote I=X∩YI=X\cap Y and

R={xi∈I∣∃xb∈Y∖X,r∈ℕ0,xi1,…,xir∈I:xb→Θxi1→Θ…→Θxir→Θxi}.R=\{x_{i}\in I\mid\exists x_{b}\in Y\setminus X,r\in\mathbb{N}_{0},x_{i_{1}},\dots,x_{i_{r}}\in I:x_{b}\overset{\Theta}{\to}x_{i_{1}}\overset{\Theta}{\to}\dots\overset{\Theta}{\to}x_{i_{r}}\overset{\Theta}{\to}x_{i}\}.

Also set S=I∖RS=I\setminus R. We denote by

M=(Y∖X)∪RandN=(X∖Y)∪S.M=(Y\setminus X)\cup R\quad\text{and}\quad N=(X\setminus Y)\cup S. (1)

Observe that since R,S⊆I=X∩YR,S\subseteq I=X\cap Y, the above unions are disjoint. Then we further have

X=N∪R,Y=M∪S,X∪Y=N∪M.X=N\cup R,\quad Y=M\cup S,\quad X\cup Y=N\cup M. (2)

The unions on the right-hand sides of these equalities are disjoint as well. The key observation is the following claim.

Claim.

There are no arrows starting in MM and ending in NN.

Proof of the claim.

We argue by contradiction. Let xi∈Mx_{i}\in M, xj∈Nx_{j}\in N and suppose xi​→Θ​xjx_{i}\overset{\Theta}{\to}x_{j}. Now we consider cases on xix_{i} and xjx_{j} based on (1). Since pΘ​(X,Y)p_{\Theta}(X,Y) holds, we cannot have xi∈Y∖Xx_{i}\in Y\setminus X and xj∈X∖Yx_{j}\in X\setminus Y. If xi∈Y∖Xx_{i}\in Y\setminus X and xj∈Sx_{j}\in S, this implies xj∈Rx_{j}\in R by the definition of RR, which is a contradiction since R∩S=∅R\cap S=\emptyset. If xi∈Rx_{i}\in R and xj∈X∖Yx_{j}\in X\setminus Y, then by the definition of RR, there exist xb∈Y∖Xx_{b}\in Y\setminus X, r∈ℕ0r\in\mathbb{N}_{0}, and xi1,…,xir∈Ix_{i_{1}},\dots,x_{i_{r}}\in I such that

xb​→Θ​xi1​→Θ​…​→Θ​xir​→Θ​xi​→Θ​xj.x_{b}\overset{\Theta}{\to}x_{i_{1}}\overset{\Theta}{\to}\dots\overset{\Theta}{\to}x_{i_{r}}\overset{\Theta}{\to}x_{i}\overset{\Theta}{\to}x_{j}.

Since xi∈R⊆Ix_{i}\in R\subseteq I and xj∈X∖Yx_{j}\in X\setminus Y, this contradicts the fact that pΘ​(X,Y)p_{\Theta}(X,Y) holds. If xi∈Rx_{i}\in R and xj∈Sx_{j}\in S, we have some xb∈Y∖Xx_{b}\in Y\setminus X, r∈ℕ0r\in\mathbb{N}_{0}, and xi1,…,xir∈Ix_{i_{1}},\dots,x_{i_{r}}\in I such that

xb​→Θ​xi1​→Θ​…​→Θ​xir​→Θ​xi​→Θ​xj.x_{b}\overset{\Theta}{\to}x_{i_{1}}\overset{\Theta}{\to}\dots\overset{\Theta}{\to}x_{i_{r}}\overset{\Theta}{\to}x_{i}\overset{\Theta}{\to}x_{j}.

Since xi∈R⊆Ix_{i}\in R\subseteq I, this implies that xj∈Rx_{j}\in R. Thus xj∈R∩Sx_{j}\in R\cap S, which is again a contradiction. The above cases are exhaustive by (1). Hence, in all cases, we have reached a contradiction, and therefore there are no arrows starting in MM and ending in NN. ∎

Since N⊆X∈𝒜ΘN\subseteq X\in\mathcal{A}_{\Theta} and M⊆Y∈𝒜ΘM\subseteq Y\in\mathcal{A}_{\Theta}, Remark 2.6 implies N,M∈𝒜ΘN,M\in\mathcal{A}_{\Theta}. Since N∩M=∅N\cap M=\emptyset and there are no arrows starting in MM and ending in NN, Lemma 2.13 yields

N∪M∈𝒜ΘandeN​eM=eN∪M.N\cup M\in\mathcal{A}_{\Theta}\quad\text{and}\quad e_{N}e_{M}=e_{N\cup M}.

Since X∪Y=N∪MX\cup Y=N\cup M by (2), we obtain

X∪Y∈𝒜ΘandeN​eM=eX∪Y.X\cup Y\in\mathcal{A}_{\Theta}\quad\text{and}\quad e_{N}e_{M}=e_{X\cup Y}. (3)

Since R,S⊆X∪Y∈𝒜ΘR,S\subseteq X\cup Y\in\mathcal{A}_{\Theta}, we also have R,S∈𝒜ΘR,S\in\mathcal{A}_{\Theta} by Remark 2.6. As R⊆MR\subseteq M and there are no arrows starting in MM and ending in NN, there are no arrows starting in RR and ending in NN. Since N∩R=∅N\cap R=\emptyset, Lemma 2.13 implies

eN​eR=eN∪R=eX.e_{N}e_{R}=e_{N\cup R}=e_{X}. (4)

Similarly, since S⊆NS\subseteq N, there are no arrows starting in MM and ending in SS. Since S∩M=∅S\cap M=\emptyset, Lemma 2.13 implies

eS​eM=eS∪M=eY.e_{S}e_{M}=e_{S\cup M}=e_{Y}. (5)

Since c⁡(eS)=S⊆Xc(e_{S})=S\subseteq X and c⁡(eR)=R⊆Mc(e_{R})=R\subseteq M, Lemma 2.9 implies

eX​eS=eXandeR​eM=eM.e_{X}e_{S}=e_{X}\quad\text{and}\quad e_{R}e_{M}=e_{M}. (6)

Using (3), (4), (5), and (6), we obtain

eX​eY=eX​eS​eM=eX​eM=eN​eR​eM=eN​eM=eX∪Y.e_{X}e_{Y}=e_{X}e_{S}e_{M}=e_{X}e_{M}=e_{N}e_{R}e_{M}=e_{N}e_{M}=e_{X\cup Y}.

This concludes the proof. ∎

Propositions 3.4 and 3.5 imply the following theorem.

Theorem 3.6.

Let X,Y∈𝒜ΘX,Y\in\mathcal{A}_{\Theta}. Then eX​eYe_{X}e_{Y} is an idempotent in 𝐇𝐊Θ\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta} if and only if pΘ​(X,Y)p_{\Theta}(X,Y) holds.

Lemma 3.7.

Let X,Y∈𝒜ΘX,Y\in\mathcal{A}_{\Theta} and assume that X∪Y∈𝒜ΘX\cup Y\in\mathcal{A}_{\Theta} as well. Then eX∪Y​eXe_{X\cup Y}e_{X} and eY​eX∪Ye_{Y}e_{X\cup Y} are idempotents in 𝐇𝐊Θ\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta}.

Proof.

Since X∖(X∪Y)=∅X\setminus(X\cup Y)=\emptyset and Y∖(X∪Y)=∅Y\setminus(X\cup Y)=\emptyset, conditions pΘ​(X∪Y,X)p_{\Theta}(X\cup Y,X) and pΘ​(Y,X∪Y)p_{\Theta}(Y,X\cup Y) vacuously hold. The conclusion follows from Theorem 3.6. ∎

Theorem 3.8.

Let X,Y∈𝒜ΘX,Y\in\mathcal{A}_{\Theta}. Then pΘ​(X,Y)p_{\Theta}(X,Y) holds if and only if

eX​eY​eX=eY​eX​eY=eX​eY.e_{X}e_{Y}e_{X}=e_{Y}e_{X}e_{Y}=e_{X}e_{Y}.
Proof.

Assume

eX​eY​eX=eY​eX​eY=eX​eYe_{X}e_{Y}e_{X}=e_{Y}e_{X}e_{Y}=e_{X}e_{Y}

holds. Then

(eX​eY)2=eX​eY​eX​eY=(eX​eY​eX)​eY=eX​eY​eY=eX​eY,(e_{X}e_{Y})^{2}=e_{X}e_{Y}e_{X}e_{Y}=(e_{X}e_{Y}e_{X})e_{Y}=e_{X}e_{Y}e_{Y}=e_{X}e_{Y},

which implies that eX​eYe_{X}e_{Y} is an idempotent, and hence by Theorem 3.6, pΘ​(X,Y)p_{\Theta}(X,Y) holds.

Conversely, assume pΘ​(X,Y)p_{\Theta}(X,Y) holds. By Theorem 3.6, eX​eYe_{X}e_{Y} is an idempotent. By Proposition 2.8, it follows that X∪Y∈𝒜ΘX\cup Y\in\mathcal{A}_{\Theta} and

eX​eY=eX∪Y.e_{X}e_{Y}=e_{X\cup Y}. (7)

Since X,Y,X∪Y∈𝒜ΘX,Y,X\cup Y\in\mathcal{A}_{\Theta}, Lemma 3.7 implies that eX∪Y​eXe_{X\cup Y}e_{X} and eY​eX∪Ye_{Y}e_{X\cup Y} are idempotents as well. By Proposition 2.8, we further have

eX∪Y​eX=e(X∪Y)∪X=eX∪YandeY​eX∪Y=eY∪(X∪Y)=eX∪Y.e_{X\cup Y}e_{X}=e_{(X\cup Y)\cup X}=e_{X\cup Y}\quad\text{and}\quad e_{Y}e_{X\cup Y}=e_{Y\cup(X\cup Y)}=e_{X\cup Y}.

Using (7), we conclude that

eX​eY​eX=eY​eX​eY=eX​eY.e_{X}e_{Y}e_{X}=e_{Y}e_{X}e_{Y}=e_{X}e_{Y}.

∎

Corollary 3.9.

Let X,Y∈𝒜ΘX,Y\in\mathcal{A}_{\Theta}. Then pΘ​(X,Y)p_{\Theta}(X,Y) and pΘ​(Y,X)p_{\Theta}(Y,X) both hold if and only if eX​eY=eY​eXe_{X}e_{Y}=e_{Y}e_{X}.

Proof.

If pΘ​(X,Y)p_{\Theta}(X,Y) and pΘ​(Y,X)p_{\Theta}(Y,X) both hold, then by Theorem 3.8, we have

eX​eY​eX=eY​eX​eY=eX​eYandeY​eX​eY=eX​eY​eX=eY​eX,e_{X}e_{Y}e_{X}=e_{Y}e_{X}e_{Y}=e_{X}e_{Y}\quad\text{and}\quad e_{Y}e_{X}e_{Y}=e_{X}e_{Y}e_{X}=e_{Y}e_{X},

which implies eX​eY=eY​eXe_{X}e_{Y}=e_{Y}e_{X}.

Conversely, if eX​eY=eY​eXe_{X}e_{Y}=e_{Y}e_{X}, then

eX​eY​eX=eX​(eY​eX)=eX​eX​eY=eX​eY=eY​eX,e_{X}e_{Y}e_{X}=e_{X}(e_{Y}e_{X})=e_{X}e_{X}e_{Y}=e_{X}e_{Y}=e_{Y}e_{X},

and

eY​eX​eY=(eY​eX)​eY=eX​eY​eY=eX​eY=eY​eX,e_{Y}e_{X}e_{Y}=(e_{Y}e_{X})e_{Y}=e_{X}e_{Y}e_{Y}=e_{X}e_{Y}=e_{Y}e_{X},

which implies

eX​eY​eX=eY​eX​eY=eX​eYandeY​eX​eY=eX​eY​eX=eY​eX.e_{X}e_{Y}e_{X}=e_{Y}e_{X}e_{Y}=e_{X}e_{Y}\quad\text{and}\quad e_{Y}e_{X}e_{Y}=e_{X}e_{Y}e_{X}=e_{Y}e_{X}.

Theorem 3.8 implies that pΘ​(X,Y)p_{\Theta}(X,Y) and pΘ​(Y,X)p_{\Theta}(Y,X) both hold. ∎

4 Homomorphisms from 𝐇𝐊Γ\mathbf{HK}_{\Gamma} to 𝐇𝐊Θ\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta}

In this section, we study the set Hom⁡(𝐇𝐊Γ,𝐇𝐊Θ)\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbf{HK}_{\Gamma},\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta}) of all monoid homomorphisms from 𝐇𝐊Γ\mathbf{HK}_{\Gamma} to 𝐇𝐊Θ\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta}.

Theorem 4.1.

Let φ:{y1,y2,…,ym}→𝐇𝐊Θ\varphi:\{y_{1},y_{2},\dots,y_{m}\}\to\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta} be a map defined on the generators of 𝐇𝐊Γ\mathbf{HK}_{\Gamma}. The map φ\varphi extends to a monoid homomorphism from 𝐇𝐊Γ\mathbf{HK}_{\Gamma} to 𝐇𝐊Θ\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta} if and only if there exist sets X1,X2,…,XmX_{1},X_{2},\dots,X_{m} with Xi⊆VΘX_{i}\subseteq V_{\Theta} such that, for all i,j∈{1,2,…,m}i,j\in\{1,2,\dots,m\}, the following conditions hold:

  1. (i)

    Xi∈𝒜ΘX_{i}\in\mathcal{A}_{\Theta};

  2. (ii)

    φ⁡(yi)=eXi\varphi(y_{i})=e_{X_{i}};

  3. (iii)

    pΘ​(Xi,Xj)p_{\Theta}(X_{i},X_{j}) and pΘ​(Xj,Xi)p_{\Theta}(X_{j},X_{i}) both hold if yiy_{i} and yjy_{j} are not connected in Γ\Gamma;

  4. (iv)

    pΘ​(Xi,Xj)p_{\Theta}(X_{i},X_{j}) holds if yi​→Γ​yjy_{i}\overset{\Gamma}{\to}y_{j}.

Proof.

Assume that the map φ\varphi extends to a monoid homomorphism from 𝐇𝐊Γ\mathbf{HK}_{\Gamma} to 𝐇𝐊Θ\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta}, which we also denote by φ\varphi. Since a monoid homomorphism maps idempotents to idempotents, φ⁡(yi)\varphi(y_{i}) is an idempotent in 𝐇𝐊Θ\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta} for all i∈{1,2,…,m}i\in\{1,2,\dots,m\}. By Proposition 2.7, φ⁡(yi)\varphi(y_{i}) is of the form eXe_{X} for some X∈𝒜ΘX\in\mathcal{A}_{\Theta}. Hence there exist sets X1,X2,…,XmX_{1},X_{2},\dots,X_{m} with Xi∈𝒜ΘX_{i}\in\mathcal{A}_{\Theta} for i∈{1,2,…,m}i\in\{1,2,\dots,m\}, such that

φ⁡(yi)=eXi,\varphi(y_{i})=e_{X_{i}},

for all i∈{1,2,…,m}i\in\{1,2,\dots,m\}, which proves (i) and (ii). Now let i,j∈{1,2,…,m}i,j\in\{1,2,\dots,m\}.

Case 1: yiy_{i} and yjy_{j} are not connected in Γ\Gamma. In this case, we have

yi​yj=yj​yi.y_{i}y_{j}=y_{j}y_{i}.

Applying φ\varphi yields

eXi​eXj=eXj​eXi.e_{X_{i}}e_{X_{j}}=e_{X_{j}}e_{X_{i}}.

Corollary 3.9 implies that pΘ​(Xi,Xj)p_{\Theta}(X_{i},X_{j}) and pΘ​(Xj,Xi)p_{\Theta}(X_{j},X_{i}) both hold. This proves (iii).

Case 2: yi​→Γ​yjy_{i}\overset{\Gamma}{\to}y_{j}. In this case, we have

yi​yj​yi=yj​yi​yj=yi​yj,y_{i}y_{j}y_{i}=y_{j}y_{i}y_{j}=y_{i}y_{j},

and hence by applying φ\varphi, we obtain

eXi​eXj​eXi=eXj​eXi​eXj=eXi​eXj.e_{X_{i}}e_{X_{j}}e_{X_{i}}=e_{X_{j}}e_{X_{i}}e_{X_{j}}=e_{X_{i}}e_{X_{j}}.

Theorem 3.8 implies that pΘ​(Xi,Xj)p_{\Theta}(X_{i},X_{j}) holds. This proves (iv).

We have proved the necessity of the condition stated in the theorem. Now we prove sufficiency. We claim that the elements φ⁡(y1),φ⁡(y2),…,φ⁡(ym)\varphi(y_{1}),\varphi(y_{2}),\dots,\varphi(y_{m}) satisfy the defining relations of 𝐇𝐊Γ\mathbf{HK}_{\Gamma}. Hence, we need to show that eX1,eX2,…,eXme_{X_{1}},e_{X_{2}},\dots,e_{X_{m}} satisfy the defining relations of 𝐇𝐊Γ\mathbf{HK}_{\Gamma}. Each eXie_{X_{i}} for i∈{1,2,…,m}i\in\{1,2,\dots,m\} is an idempotent by Proposition 2.7. Let i,j∈{1,2,…,m}i,j\in\{1,2,\dots,m\}.

Case 1: yiy_{i} and yjy_{j} are not connected in Γ\Gamma. We need to show that

eXi​eXj=eXj​eXi.e_{X_{i}}e_{X_{j}}=e_{X_{j}}e_{X_{i}}.

By assumption, pΘ​(Xi,Xj)p_{\Theta}(X_{i},X_{j}) and pΘ​(Xj,Xi)p_{\Theta}(X_{j},X_{i}) both hold, and hence the desired equality follows from Corollary 3.9.

Case 2: yi​→Γ​yjy_{i}\overset{\Gamma}{\to}y_{j}. We need to show that

eXi​eXj​eXi=eXj​eXi​eXj=eXi​eXj.e_{X_{i}}e_{X_{j}}e_{X_{i}}=e_{X_{j}}e_{X_{i}}e_{X_{j}}=e_{X_{i}}e_{X_{j}}.

By assumption, pΘ​(Xi,Xj)p_{\Theta}(X_{i},X_{j}) holds, and hence the desired equality follows from Theorem 3.8.

Hence, the elements φ⁡(y1),φ⁡(y2),…,φ⁡(ym)\varphi(y_{1}),\varphi(y_{2}),\dots,\varphi(y_{m}) satisfy the defining relations of 𝐇𝐊Γ\mathbf{HK}_{\Gamma}, and thus we can extend φ\varphi to a monoid homomorphism from 𝐇𝐊Γ\mathbf{HK}_{\Gamma} to 𝐇𝐊Θ\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta}. ∎

Denote by

𝒮Γ,Θ={(X1,X2,…,Xm)∣Xi⊆VΘ​ for ​i∈{1,2,…,m}},\mathcal{S}_{\Gamma,\Theta}=\{(X_{1},X_{2},\dots,X_{m})\mid X_{i}\subseteq V_{\Theta}\text{ for }i\in\{1,2,\dots,m\}\},

the set of all sequences of length mm of subsets of VΘV_{\Theta}.

Definition 4.2.

A sequence (X1,X2,…,Xm)(X_{1},X_{2},\dots,X_{m}) of length mm of subsets of VΘV_{\Theta} is said to be (Γ,Θ)(\Gamma,\Theta)-admissible if, for all i,j∈{1,2,…,m}i,j\in\{1,2,\dots,m\}, the following conditions hold:

  1. (i)

    Xi∈𝒜ΘX_{i}\in\mathcal{A}_{\Theta};

  2. (ii)

    pΘ​(Xi,Xj)p_{\Theta}(X_{i},X_{j}) and pΘ​(Xj,Xi)p_{\Theta}(X_{j},X_{i}) both hold if yiy_{i} and yjy_{j} are not connected in Γ\Gamma;

  3. (iii)

    pΘ​(Xi,Xj)p_{\Theta}(X_{i},X_{j}) holds if yi​→Γ​yjy_{i}\overset{\Gamma}{\to}y_{j}.

We also define

𝒮~Γ,Θ={(X1,X2,…,Xm)∈𝒮Γ,Θ∣(X1,X2,…,Xm)​ is (Γ,Θ)-admissible},\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}_{\Gamma,\Theta}=\{(X_{1},X_{2},\dots,X_{m})\in\mathcal{S}_{\Gamma,\Theta}\mid(X_{1},X_{2},\dots,X_{m})\text{ is $(\Gamma,\Theta)$-admissible}\},

and the map Φ:Hom⁡(𝐇𝐊Γ,𝐇𝐊Θ)→𝒮Γ,Θ\Phi:\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbf{HK}_{\Gamma},\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta})\to\mathcal{S}_{\Gamma,\Theta} by

Φ⁡(φ)=(c⁡(φ⁡(y1)),c⁡(φ⁡(y2)),…,c⁡(φ⁡(ym))).\Phi(\varphi)=\big(c(\varphi(y_{1})),c(\varphi(y_{2})),\dots,c(\varphi(y_{m}))\big).
Proposition 4.3.

The map Φ:Hom⁡(𝐇𝐊Γ,𝐇𝐊Θ)→𝒮~Γ,Θ\Phi:\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbf{HK}_{\Gamma},\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta})\to\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}_{\Gamma,\Theta} is a bijection.

Proof.

Let φ∈Hom⁡(𝐇𝐊Γ,𝐇𝐊Θ)\varphi\in\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbf{HK}_{\Gamma},\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta}). By Theorem 4.1, there exists a (Γ,Θ)(\Gamma,\Theta)-admissible sequence (X1,X2,…,Xm)(X_{1},X_{2},\dots,X_{m}) such that

φ⁡(yi)=eXi,\varphi(y_{i})=e_{X_{i}},

for all i∈{1,2,…,m}i\in\{1,2,\dots,m\}. Hence,

Φ⁡(φ)=(c⁡(φ⁡(y1)),c⁡(φ⁡(y2)),…,c⁡(φ⁡(ym)))=(X1,X2,…,Xm),\Phi(\varphi)=(c(\varphi(y_{1})),c(\varphi(y_{2})),\dots,c(\varphi(y_{m})))=(X_{1},X_{2},\dots,X_{m}),

which proves that Φ\Phi maps into 𝒮~Γ,Θ\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}_{\Gamma,\Theta}.

Since every homomorphism from 𝐇𝐊Γ\mathbf{HK}_{\Gamma} to 𝐇𝐊Θ\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta} is uniquely determined by the images of the generators, since every homomorphism from 𝐇𝐊Γ\mathbf{HK}_{\Gamma} to 𝐇𝐊Θ\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta} maps generators to idempotents, and since idempotents in 𝐇𝐊Θ\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta} are uniquely determined by their content, Φ\Phi is injective.

Let (X1,X2,…,Xm)∈𝒮~Γ,Θ(X_{1},X_{2},\dots,X_{m})\in\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}_{\Gamma,\Theta}. By Theorem 4.1, the map yi↦eXiy_{i}\mapsto e_{X_{i}} extends to a monoid homomorphism φ\varphi from 𝐇𝐊Γ\mathbf{HK}_{\Gamma} to 𝐇𝐊Θ\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta}. Since c⁡(φ⁡(yi))=c⁡(eXi)=Xic(\varphi(y_{i}))=c(e_{X_{i}})=X_{i} for i∈{1,2,…,m}i\in\{1,2,\dots,m\}, we obtain Φ⁡(φ)=(X1,X2,…,Xm)\Phi(\varphi)=(X_{1},X_{2},\dots,X_{m}), and hence surjectivity follows. ∎

Now we denote by ℬn,m\mathcal{B}_{n,m} the set of all n×mn\times m Boolean matrices, that is, n×mn\times m matrices with entries 00 or 11. For A∈ℬn,mA\in\mathcal{B}_{n,m}, i∈{1,2,…,n}i\in\{1,2,\dots,n\}, and j∈{1,2,…,m}j\in\{1,2,\dots,m\}, denote by Ai,jA_{i,j} the (i,j)(i,j) entry of AA. We define the map Ψ:𝒮Γ,Θ→ℬn,m\Psi:\mathcal{S}_{\Gamma,\Theta}\to\mathcal{B}_{n,m} by

Ψ​(X1,X2,…,Xm)i,j={1,xi∈Xj,0,xi∉Xj,\Psi(X_{1},X_{2},\dots,X_{m})_{i,j}=\begin{cases}1,&x_{i}\in X_{j},\\ 0,&x_{i}\notin X_{j},\end{cases}

for all i∈{1,2,…,n}i\in\{1,2,\dots,n\} and j∈{1,2,…,m}j\in\{1,2,\dots,m\}. The map Ψ\Psi has a particularly simple interpretation; it encodes, in matrix form, which elements are contained in each set of the sequence.

Proposition 4.4.

The map Ψ:𝒮Γ,Θ→ℬn,m\Psi:\mathcal{S}_{\Gamma,\Theta}\to\mathcal{B}_{n,m} is a bijection.

Proof.

The proof is immediate from the definition of Ψ\Psi. ∎

Theorem 4.5.

The map Ψ∘Φ:Hom⁡(𝐇𝐊Γ,𝐇𝐊Θ)→Ψ⁡(𝒮~Γ,Θ)\Psi\circ\Phi:\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbf{HK}_{\Gamma},\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta})\to\Psi(\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}_{\Gamma,\Theta}) is a bijection.

Proof.

By Proposition 4.3, Φ:Hom⁡(𝐇𝐊Γ,𝐇𝐊Θ)→𝒮~Γ,Θ\Phi:\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbf{HK}_{\Gamma},\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta})\to\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}_{\Gamma,\Theta} is a bijection. By Proposition 4.4, Ψ\Psi is bijective, and since 𝒮~Γ,Θ⊆𝒮Γ,Θ\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}_{\Gamma,\Theta}\subseteq\mathcal{S}_{\Gamma,\Theta}, it follows that Ψ|𝒮~Γ,Θ:𝒮~Γ,Θ→Ψ⁡(𝒮~Γ,Θ)\Psi|_{\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}_{\Gamma,\Theta}}:\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}_{\Gamma,\Theta}\to\Psi(\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}_{\Gamma,\Theta}) is a bijection. Therefore, Ψ∘Φ\Psi\circ\Phi is a bijection from Hom⁡(𝐇𝐊Γ,𝐇𝐊Θ)\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbf{HK}_{\Gamma},\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta}) to Ψ⁡(𝒮~Γ,Θ)\Psi(\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}_{\Gamma,\Theta}). ∎

5 Endomorphisms of 𝐇𝐊Θ\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta}

Here, we study the endomorphism monoid End⁡(𝐇𝐊Θ)\mathrm{End}(\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta}). We use results from Section 4 in the special case when Γ=Θ\Gamma=\Theta. In this case, we have m=nm=n and yi=xiy_{i}=x_{i} for i=1,2,…,ni=1,2,\dots,n.

The following definitions and statements are very similar to the results in Andrenšek (2026). We prove these results again because the results in Andrenšek (2026) were derived for the Kiselman monoid, which is a special case of 𝐇𝐊Θ\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta}. For completeness, we include the proofs here for 𝐇𝐊Θ\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta}.

For 𝐗=(X1,X2,…,Xn)∈𝒮Θ,Θ\mathbf{X}=(X_{1},X_{2},\dots,X_{n})\in\mathcal{S}_{\Theta,\Theta}, denote by 𝐗i=Xi\mathbf{X}_{i}=X_{i} for i∈{1,2,…,n}i\in\{1,2,\dots,n\}. We define the binary operation ∗\ast on 𝒮Θ,Θ\mathcal{S}_{\Theta,\Theta} as follows. Let (X1,X2,…,Xn)(X_{1},X_{2},\dots,X_{n}) and (Y1,Y2,…,Yn)(Y_{1},Y_{2},\dots,Y_{n}) be elements of 𝒮Θ,Θ\mathcal{S}_{\Theta,\Theta}. Then we set

(X1,X2,…,Xn)∗(Y1,Y2,…,Yn)=(⋃xj∈Y1Xj,⋃xj∈Y2Xj,…,⋃xj∈YnXj).(X_{1},X_{2},\dots,X_{n})\ast(Y_{1},Y_{2},\dots,Y_{n})=(\bigcup_{x_{j}\in Y_{1}}X_{j},\bigcup_{x_{j}\in Y_{2}}X_{j},\dots,\bigcup_{x_{j}\in Y_{n}}X_{j}).

It quickly follows that (𝒮Θ,Θ,∗)(\mathcal{S}_{\Theta,\Theta},\ast) is a monoid with unit element ({x1},{x2},…,{xn})(\{x_{1}\},\{x_{2}\},\dots,\{x_{n}\}).

Proposition 5.1.

The map Φ:End⁡(𝐇𝐊Θ)→𝒮Θ,Θ\Phi:\mathrm{End}(\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta})\to\mathcal{S}_{\Theta,\Theta} is a monoid homomorphism from End⁡(𝐇𝐊Θ)\mathrm{End}(\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta}) to (𝒮Θ,Θ,∗)(\mathcal{S}_{\Theta,\Theta},\ast).

Proof.

Let ψ,φ∈End⁡(𝐇𝐊Θ)\psi,\varphi\in\mathrm{End}(\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta}) and let i∈{1,2,…,n}i\in\{1,2,\dots,n\}. By Lemma 2.1, we have

(Φ⁡(ψ∘φ))i=c⁡((ψ∘φ)​(xi))=⋃xj∈c⁡(φ⁡(xi))c⁡(ψ⁡(xj)).(\Phi(\psi\circ\varphi))_{i}=c((\psi\circ\varphi)(x_{i}))=\bigcup_{x_{j}\in c(\varphi(x_{i}))}c(\psi(x_{j})).

We also have

(Φ⁡(ψ)∗Φ⁡(φ))i\displaystyle\big(\Phi(\psi)\ast\Phi(\varphi)\big)_{i} =((c⁡(ψ⁡(x1)),…,c⁡(ψ⁡(xn)))∗(c⁡(φ⁡(x1)),…,c⁡(φ⁡(xn))))i\displaystyle=\big((c(\psi(x_{1})),\dots,c(\psi(x_{n})))\ast(c(\varphi(x_{1})),\dots,c(\varphi(x_{n})))\big)_{i}
=⋃xj∈c⁡(φ⁡(xi))c⁡(ψ⁡(xj)).\displaystyle=\bigcup_{x_{j}\in c(\varphi(x_{i}))}c(\psi(x_{j})).

We thus have

(Φ⁡(ψ∘φ))i=(Φ⁡(ψ)∗Φ⁡(φ))i.\big(\Phi(\psi\circ\varphi)\big)_{i}=\big(\Phi(\psi)\ast\Phi(\varphi)\big)_{i}.

It follows that

Φ⁡(ψ∘φ)=Φ⁡(ψ)∗Φ⁡(φ).\displaystyle\Phi(\psi\circ\varphi)=\Phi(\psi)\ast\Phi(\varphi).

Moreover, since the identity map is the unit element of End⁡(𝐇𝐊Θ)\mathrm{End}(\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta}) and

Φ⁡(id𝐇𝐊Θ)=({x1},{x2},…,{xn}),\displaystyle\Phi(\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta}})=(\{x_{1}\},\{x_{2}\},\dots,\{x_{n}\}),

we conclude that Φ\Phi is a monoid homomorphism. ∎

We define the binary operation ⋅\cdot on ℬn,n\mathcal{B}_{n,n} as follows. Let A,B∈ℬn,nA,B\in\mathcal{B}_{n,n}. Then C=A⋅BC=A\cdot B, with

Ci,j=⋁k=1n(Ai,k∧Bk,j),\displaystyle C_{i,j}=\bigvee_{k=1}^{n}(A_{i,k}\land B_{k,j}),

for all i,j∈{1,2,…,n}i,j\in\{1,2,\dots,n\}. Here, ∨\lor denotes the Boolean join and ∧\land denotes the Boolean meet on {0,1}\{0,1\}. One can easily check that (ℬn,n,⋅)(\mathcal{B}_{n,n},\cdot) is a monoid, and its unit element is the identity matrix II of size n×nn\times n.

Proposition 5.2.

The map Ψ:𝒮Θ,Θ→ℬn,n\Psi:\mathcal{S}_{\Theta,\Theta}\to\mathcal{B}_{n,n} is a monoid homomorphism from (𝒮Θ,Θ,∗)(\mathcal{S}_{\Theta,\Theta},\ast) to (ℬn,n,⋅)(\mathcal{B}_{n,n},\cdot).

Proof.

Let 𝐗,𝐘∈𝒮Θ,Θ\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y}\in\mathcal{S}_{\Theta,\Theta}, where 𝐗=(X1,X2,…,Xn)\mathbf{X}=(X_{1},X_{2},\dots,X_{n}) and 𝐘=(Y1,Y2,…,Yn)\mathbf{Y}=(Y_{1},Y_{2},\dots,Y_{n}). We compute

Ψ⁡(𝐗∗𝐘)=Ψ⁡(⋃xj∈Y1Xj,⋃xj∈Y2Xj,…,⋃xj∈YnXj).\Psi(\mathbf{X}\ast\mathbf{Y})=\Psi(\bigcup_{x_{j}\in Y_{1}}X_{j},\bigcup_{x_{j}\in Y_{2}}X_{j},\dots,\bigcup_{x_{j}\in Y_{n}}X_{j}).

It follows that for i,j∈{1,2,…,n}i,j\in\{1,2,\dots,n\} we have

Ψ​(𝐗∗𝐘)i,j=1\displaystyle\Psi(\mathbf{X}\ast\mathbf{Y})_{i,j}=1 ⇔xi∈⋃xl∈YjXl\displaystyle\iff x_{i}\in\bigcup_{x_{l}\in Y_{j}}X_{l}
⇔there exists ​xk∈Yj​ such that ​xi∈Xk.\displaystyle\iff\text{there exists }x_{k}\in Y_{j}\text{ such that }x_{i}\in X_{k}.

On the other hand,

(Ψ⁡(𝐗)⋅Ψ⁡(𝐘))i,j=⋁k=1n(Ψ​(𝐗)i,k∧Ψ​(𝐘)k,j).(\Psi(\mathbf{X})\cdot\Psi(\mathbf{Y}))_{i,j}=\bigvee_{k=1}^{n}(\Psi(\mathbf{X})_{i,k}\land\Psi(\mathbf{Y})_{k,j}).

Hence, we have

(Ψ⁡(𝐗)⋅Ψ⁡(𝐘))i,j=1\displaystyle(\Psi(\mathbf{X})\cdot\Psi(\mathbf{Y}))_{i,j}=1 ⇔there exists ​k∈{1,2,…,n}​ such that ​Ψ​(𝐗)i,k=Ψ​(𝐘)k,j=1\displaystyle\iff\text{there exists }k\in\{1,2,\dots,n\}\text{ such that }\Psi(\mathbf{X})_{i,k}=\Psi(\mathbf{Y})_{k,j}=1
⇔there exists ​k∈{1,2,…,n}​ such that ​xi∈Xk​ and ​xk∈Yj\displaystyle\iff\text{there exists }k\in\{1,2,\dots,n\}\text{ such that }x_{i}\in X_{k}\text{ and }x_{k}\in Y_{j}
⇔there exists ​xk∈Yj​ such that ​xi∈Xk.\displaystyle\iff\text{there exists }x_{k}\in Y_{j}\text{ such that }x_{i}\in X_{k}.

We thus obtain

Ψ​(𝐗∗𝐘)i,j=1⇔(Ψ⁡(𝐗)⋅Ψ⁡(𝐘))i,j=1,\Psi(\mathbf{X}\ast\mathbf{Y})_{i,j}=1\iff(\Psi(\mathbf{X})\cdot\Psi(\mathbf{Y}))_{i,j}=1,

and since Ψ⁡(𝐗∗𝐘)\Psi(\mathbf{X}\ast\mathbf{Y}) and Ψ⁡(𝐗)⋅Ψ⁡(𝐘)\Psi(\mathbf{X})\cdot\Psi(\mathbf{Y}) are both Boolean matrices, we get

Ψ​(𝐗∗𝐘)i,j=(Ψ⁡(𝐗)⋅Ψ⁡(𝐘))i,j.\Psi(\mathbf{X}\ast\mathbf{Y})_{i,j}=(\Psi(\mathbf{X})\cdot\Psi(\mathbf{Y}))_{i,j}.

Since ii and jj are arbitrary, it follows that

Ψ⁡(𝐗∗𝐘)=Ψ⁡(𝐗)⋅Ψ⁡(𝐘).\Psi(\mathbf{X}\ast\mathbf{Y})=\Psi(\mathbf{X})\cdot\Psi(\mathbf{Y}).

Furthermore, since Ψ⁡({x1},{x2},…,{xn})=I\Psi(\{x_{1}\},\{x_{2}\},\dots,\{x_{n}\})=I, it follows that Ψ\Psi is a monoid homomorphism. ∎

Theorem 5.3.

The map Ψ∘Φ:End⁡(𝐇𝐊Θ)→ℬn,n\Psi\circ\Phi:\mathrm{End}(\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta})\to\mathcal{B}_{n,n} is a monoid homomorphism from End⁡(𝐇𝐊Θ)\mathrm{End}(\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta}) to (ℬn,n,⋅)(\mathcal{B}_{n,n},\cdot).

Proof.

The proof is immediate from Propositions 5.1 and 5.2, and the fact that a composition of monoid homomorphisms is a monoid homomorphism. ∎

Theorem 5.4.

The set Ψ⁡(𝒮~Θ,Θ)\Psi(\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}_{\Theta,\Theta}), equipped with the operation ⋅\cdot, is a monoid and we have

End⁡(𝐇𝐊Θ)≅(Ψ⁡(𝒮~Θ,Θ),⋅),\mathrm{End}(\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta})\cong(\Psi(\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}_{\Theta,\Theta}),\cdot),

where the corresponding monoid isomorphism is given by Ψ∘Φ\Psi\circ\Phi.

Proof.

By Theorem 4.5, Ψ∘Φ:End⁡(𝐇𝐊Θ)→Ψ⁡(𝒮~Θ,Θ)\Psi\circ\Phi:\mathrm{End}(\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta})\to\Psi(\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}_{\Theta,\Theta}) is a bijection. Pick any A,B∈Ψ⁡(𝒮~Θ,Θ)A,B\in\Psi(\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}_{\Theta,\Theta}). Then there exist ψ,φ∈End⁡(𝐇𝐊Θ)\psi,\varphi\in\mathrm{End}(\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta}) such that

(Ψ∘Φ)​(ψ)=Aand(Ψ∘Φ)​(φ)=B.(\Psi\circ\Phi)(\psi)=A\quad\text{and}\quad(\Psi\circ\Phi)(\varphi)=B.

Using Theorem 5.3, we conclude that

A⋅B=(Ψ∘Φ)​(ψ)⋅(Ψ∘Φ)​(φ)=(Ψ∘Φ)​(ψ∘φ)∈Ψ⁡(𝒮~Θ,Θ),A\cdot B=(\Psi\circ\Phi)(\psi)\cdot(\Psi\circ\Phi)(\varphi)=(\Psi\circ\Phi)(\psi\circ\varphi)\in\Psi(\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}_{\Theta,\Theta}),

since ψ∘φ∈End⁡(𝐇𝐊Θ)\psi\circ\varphi\in\mathrm{End}(\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta}). This shows that Ψ⁡(𝒮~Θ,Θ)\Psi(\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}_{\Theta,\Theta}) is closed under ⋅\cdot. Since

I=(Ψ∘Φ)​(id𝐇𝐊Θ)∈Ψ⁡(𝒮~Θ,Θ),I=(\Psi\circ\Phi)(\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta}})\in\Psi(\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}_{\Theta,\Theta}),

it follows that (Ψ⁡(𝒮~Θ,Θ),⋅)(\Psi(\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}_{\Theta,\Theta}),\cdot) is a submonoid of (ℬn,n,⋅)(\mathcal{B}_{n,n},\cdot), and

Ψ∘Φ:End⁡(𝐇𝐊Θ)→Ψ⁡(𝒮~Θ,Θ)\Psi\circ\Phi:\mathrm{End}(\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta})\to\Psi(\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}_{\Theta,\Theta})

is an isomorphism of monoids from End⁡(𝐇𝐊Θ)\mathrm{End}(\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta}) to (Ψ⁡(𝒮~Θ,Θ),⋅)(\Psi(\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}_{\Theta,\Theta}),\cdot) by Theorems 4.5 and 5.3. ∎
